(CNN) -- The September issue of Essence magazine features an interview with Sen. Barack Obama and his family inside their Chicago home. Angela Burt-Murray is editor-in-chief of Essence magazine. Essence editor-in-chief Angela Burt-Murray said it took a year for the magazine to gain access to the Obama's Illinois home for an intimate interview with the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, his wife, Michelle, and their daughters, Sasha and Malia. Burt-Murray talked Thursday with CNN "American Morning" anchor Kiran Chetry about the interview and the Obama family. Chetry: You are the first African-American media outlet to get this inside look. Did your team get a chance to see the real Obamas? Burt-Murray: I think we did. We went to their home on the South Side of Chicago and it was wonderful to see them as a family interacting with each other, and see the girls skipping around the house, just acting like it's a normal, everyday occurrence to have a camera crew in their home and Secret Service at different points throughout the house and around the yard. But it didn't really seem to impact the girls in any way.  Watch what Essence found inside the Obamas' home » . Chetry: Much was made of an earlier televised interview they with their daughters and they said, looking back, they probably shouldn't have done that. There is so much interest about their family, and yet they want to protect their girls. How do they balance that? Burt-Murray: They try to take a look at who is around the family and make sure they try to keep things as structured as possible. But also, you have instances where magazines like Essence show up to take photographs, but the girls are very relaxed because they're in their home environment. And I think that's the difference between our photo shoot and what you saw on television. Taking the girls outside of their home and putting them in the spotlight is probably a bit more challenging for them as parents. Chetry: They have to deal with completing stereotypes, if you will: They were parodied as these angry black radicals and as these Ivy League elitists. In the magazine, Gwen Ifill wrote, "The Obamas pride themselves on creating a family picture that is authentically black with shades of Norman Rockwell." Explain that. How are they getting that image out. Burt-Murray: I think it's the idea that they're just an average American family. They have strong family values, they're deeply rooted in their community and they want to show their girls a great example of achievement. But they also want to be a model for the rest of their community. The Obamas talk about in our story how important it is for them to continue to live in their South Side Chicago neighborhood because it's a neighborhood in transition. So you have children who have the opportunity to see an African-American man run for the highest office in the nation right in their neighborhood. So they're modeling not only for their children but also for the larger community. Chetry: They do live in a gated community, a $1.6 million home, so it's out of reach for a lot of people. Burt-Murray: But it's so accessible. While we were there photographing them for Essence, you could see the cars going by and stopping and people getting out to take photographs. The girls were on the porch and people could see them. There is some normalcy there, but it's also obviously something very special and different. Chetry: They said race had been prominent on the campaign trail. Barack Obama told Gwen Ifill that he thinks race is a national obsession. He thinks the racial divide is not as big an issue in this country as it's made out to be. Burt-Murray: As evidenced by the success that he's had with his campaign, you can certainly see that attitudes are shifting. But there are still challenges, obviously, that need to be addressed. And it keeps coming up throughout the campaign. So it will be interesting to see what happens when the country goes to the polls in November.

Angela Burt-Murray, editor-in-chief of Essence magazine, revealed that it took a full year for the publication to secure access for this intimate profile of the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, his wife Michelle, and their daughters, Sasha and Malia. Burt-Murray spoke with CNN "American Morning" anchor Kiran Chetry on Thursday about the interview and her impressions of the Obama family.

**Chetry:** Yours is the first African-American media outlet to gain this inside look. Did your team get a genuine glimpse of the real Obamas?

**Burt-Murray:** I believe we did. We visited their home on Chicago's South Side, and it was truly wonderful to observe them interacting as a family—watching the girls skip around the house as though having a camera crew inside their home, along with Secret Service agents stationed throughout the house and yard, was simply an ordinary, everyday occurrence. It didn't seem to faze the girls in the least.

*Watch what Essence found inside the Obamas' home »*

**Chetry:** There was considerable attention surrounding an earlier televised interview featuring their daughters—one the Obamas later said, in hindsight, they probably shouldn't have done. Given the intense public interest in their family, how do they balance that scrutiny with their desire to protect their girls?

**Burt-Murray:** They're mindful of who has access to the family and strive to maintain as much structure as possible. That said, situations differ—when a publication like Essence visits for a photo shoot, the girls remain relaxed because they're within their own home environment. That's the key distinction between our shoot and what viewers saw on television. Taking the girls outside their familiar surroundings and placing them in the public eye presents a far greater challenge for the Obamas as parents.

**Chetry:** The family has had to contend with conflicting stereotypes—portrayed at various times as angry Black radicals and as Ivy League elitists. In the magazine, Gwen Ifill writes: "The Obamas pride themselves on creating a family picture that is authentically Black with shades of Norman Rockwell." Could you elaborate on that characterization and how the family conveys this image?

**Burt-Murray:** I think it reflects the idea that they're fundamentally an average American family—one grounded in strong values and deeply rooted in their community, striving to set a powerful example of achievement for their daughters. At the same time, they aspire to serve as a model for the broader community. The Obamas discuss in our story how important it is for them to continue living in their South Side Chicago neighborhood, precisely because it's a community in transition. This gives local children the opportunity to witness, firsthand in their own neighborhood, an African-American man running for the nation's highest office. In this way, the Obamas are setting an example not only for their own children, but for the wider community as well.

**Chetry:** Yet they do reside in a gated community, in a $1.6 million home—circumstances that remain out of reach for most Americans.

**Burt-Murray:** Even so, there's a remarkable accessibility to their lives. While we were there photographing them for Essence, we could see cars slowing down and passersby stopping to take photographs. The girls sat out on the porch, visible to anyone passing by. There's a certain normalcy to it, even as it's clearly something quite special and distinctive.

**Chetry:** They've noted that race has been a prominent theme throughout the campaign. Barack Obama told Gwen Ifill that he views race as something of a national obsession, and that he believes the racial divide in this country isn't as significant as it's often portrayed to be.

**Burt-Murray:** The success he's achieved with his campaign is itself evidence that attitudes are shifting. That said, real challenges clearly remain to be addressed, and the issue continues to resurface throughout the campaign. It will be fascinating to see how this all plays out when the country goes to the polls in November.

counterfactuals.output:
# Essence magazine's Obama family exclusive puts spotlight on future first family

**(CNN)** -- As the 2008 presidential campaign heads into its final stretch, Essence magazine is giving readers an intimate look at the family life of Democratic nominee Barack Obama in its September issue, hitting newsstands this week. CNN spoke with Essence Editor-in-Chief Angela Burt-Murray about the exclusive feature and what readers can expect.

The cover story, which includes new photographs and interviews, explores the Obama family dynamic -- from Michelle Obama's role as mother and potential first lady to the influence of Michelle's mother, Marian Robinson, who has been a steady presence on the campaign trail helping care for daughters Malia and Sasha.

Below is an edited transcript of the conversation.

**CNN: Angela, thanks for joining us. Tell us about the decision to focus this issue on the Obama family rather than the campaign itself.**

**BURT-MURRAY:** Thank you for having me. You know, our readers have seen wall-to-wall political coverage for over a year now -- the polls, the debates, the strategy. What Essence wanted to do was pull back the curtain a little bit and show people who this family is when the cameras aren't rolling for a stump speech. We wanted to explore what it means for a woman like Michelle Obama, a strong, accomplished black woman, to be balancing motherhood, marriage and potentially the most scrutinized job in America.

**CNN: What surprised you most in putting this feature together?**

**BURT-MURRAY:** Honestly, how much the family leans on each other. Marian Robinson has really become the anchor of that household while Barack and Michelle are out campaigning. She moved into their Chicago home, essentially traded in her own quiet retirement to make sure Malia and Sasha have consistency -- the same school, the same bedtime, the same sense of normalcy. I think that's a story a lot of our readers can relate to, that idea of grandmothers holding families together.

**CNN: Michelle Obama has faced some criticism during the campaign, being called unpatriotic by some critics after certain remarks. Does the piece address that?**

**BURT-MURRAY:** We touch on it, but we didn't want this to be a piece about controversy. We wanted to humanize her. Our readers -- Essence readers, black women across this country -- have seen themselves in Michelle Obama since day one. She's Ivy League-educated, she's a mother, she's a wife, she's someone who has had to defend herself in a way that a lot of professional black women understand intimately. So rather than relitigate the flag pin moments or the "proud of my country" comments, we wanted to show the fuller picture.

**CNN: There's been a lot of discussion about what an Obama presidency would mean symbolically for African-American families. Did that come up in your interviews?**

**BURT-MURRAY:** Absolutely. This is bigger than politics for a lot of our audience. Regardless of where people fall ideologically, there is a real sense of history happening. To potentially have a black family in the White House -- two little girls playing on the South Lawn, a grandmother from the South Side of Chicago as a fixture in the residence -- that carries weight. We wanted our September issue to capture that moment, not just as a political story, but as a cultural one.

**CNN: What do you hope readers take away from this issue?**

**BURT-MURRAY:** I hope they come away seeing the Obamas as a family first. Yes, Barack Obama is running for president, and yes, that's historic and important. But at the end of the day, this is a marriage, this is two parents trying to raise young daughters with some sense of normal childhood in an incredibly abnormal situation. I think there's something universal in that, no matter who you're voting for in November.

**CNN: Angela Burt-Murray, editor-in-chief of Essence magazine, thank you so much for your time.**

**BURT-MURRAY:** Thank you for having me.

---

*Essence magazine's September issue is available on newsstands now. CNN will continue to follow campaign coverage of both the Obama and McCain campaigns as Election Day approaches.*

# CNN American Morning
**Segment: Inside the Obama Household**
*Transcript excerpt*

---

**KIRAN CHETRY:** Welcome back. As the country gets to know Barack Obama the candidate, there's growing interest in Barack Obama the family man. Essence magazine recently got rare access to the Obama home in Chicago. Joining us now is an editor from Essence to talk about what they found. Thanks for being with us this morning.

**ESSENCE EDITOR:** Thank you for having me, Kiran. It was such a great opportunity for us.

**CHETRY:** So set the scene for us. What was it like walking into the Obama home?

**EDITOR:** You know, it's a beautiful home in the Kenwood neighborhood on the South Side of Chicago, but what struck us most was how normal it felt. There were school papers on the refrigerator, sneakers by the door. Michelle Obama really wanted us to see the family as they are when the cameras aren't typically rolling.

**CHETRY:** And we've heard so much about Michelle Obama as "the closer" on the campaign trail, but what's she like as a mom in that household?

**EDITOR:** She's very hands-on. She talked to us about keeping the girls, Malia and Sasha, grounded despite everything happening around them. Grandma — Michelle's mother — is a big presence too, helping hold things together while both parents have such demanding schedules.

**CHETRY:** Did Senator Obama talk about the balancing act — being a present father while running for president?

**EDITOR:** He did. He was candid about the guilt he feels being away so much, but he said phone calls every night are non-negotiable. He wants to hear about their day, their homework, everything. It was clear this is a man trying very hard not to miss the small moments.

**CHETRY:** Any surprising details that stood out to you personally?

**EDITOR:** I think people would be surprised by how much structure there is. Bedtimes, chores, screen time limits — Michelle's very intentional about it. She said she wants the girls raised the same way regardless of what's happening in the political world around them.

**CHETRY:** Fascinating stuff. It'll definitely give voters a different lens into who these candidates are at home. Thanks so much for joining us this morning.

**EDITOR:** Thank you, Kiran.

**CHETRY:** We'll be right back after the break.

# CNN American Morning
## Segment Transcript - Family Values: The Obama Daughters Cover Story

**KIRAN CHETRY:** Welcome back to American Morning. Barack Obama is on the cover of Essence magazine this month, but this isn't your typical political cover story. The piece focuses on his role as a father to daughters Malia and Sasha. Joining us now is the editor-in-chief of Essence magazine. Thanks so much for being with us this morning.

**EDITOR:** Thank you for having me, Kiran. It's a pleasure.

**CHETRY:** So tell us about the decision to focus this cover story specifically on fatherhood rather than the campaign trail issues we've been hearing so much about.

**EDITOR:** Well, we felt like there was a story that wasn't being told. Everyone's talking about the polls, the primaries, the debates - but our readers, particularly our audience of women, wanted to know: who is this man as a father? What does he teach his daughters? How does he balance being one of the most scrutinized men in America with just being "Dad"?

**CHETRY:** And what did you find? What surprised you most in putting this piece together?

**EDITOR:** Honestly, the normalcy of it. He talked about pancakes on Saturday mornings, about reading to the girls before bed when he's home, about Michelle really running point on discipline and structure. There's this moment where he talks about trying to explain to Malia why strangers are taking his picture, and how he wants to protect that childhood innocence for as long as possible.

**CHETRY:** That's got to be a challenge, raising young children in the spotlight of a presidential campaign.

**EDITOR:** Absolutely. And that's part of why this resonated so much with our staff and why we felt it was an Essence story. This is a Black father, talking openly about love, presence, responsibility - breaking through so many stereotypes that unfortunately still exist in media narratives about Black fatherhood.

**CHETRY:** Do you see this as political at all, or purely a human interest piece?

**EDITOR:** I think it's both, whether we intend it to be or not. The personal is political this election cycle. But our angle was really about representation - showing our readers a full, three-dimensional picture of a man who could be the next president, but who first and foremost describes himself as a father trying to get it right.

**CHETRY:** Well, it's a fascinating read. Thanks so much for joining us this morning to talk about it.

**EDITOR:** Thank you, Kiran. Appreciate the time.

**CHETRY:** Coming up next, we're going to shift gears and talk about gas prices, which are hitting record highs again this week...

*[SEGMENT ENDS]*

# Essence Magazine's Exclusive Access to the Obama Family Sparks Media Buzz

In a media landscape hungry for glimpses into the private life of the First Family, Essence magazine secured a coveted exclusive photo shoot with the Obama family, generating significant attention across news outlets. The story of how the publication—long celebrated for centering Black voices and culture—gained this rare access became a talking point in its own right, prompting a CNN interview with the magazine's editor-in-chief that illuminated both the negotiation process and its cultural significance.

**A Rare Opportunity**

Landing time with the Obamas has never been simple, even for major outlets with vast resources. For Essence, the opportunity represented something larger than a typical celebrity profile—it was a chance to present an intimate, culturally resonant portrait of a family whose historic presence in the White House carried profound meaning for its readership.

**The CNN Conversation**

During a segment addressing the exclusive, a CNN anchor sat down with the editor-in-chief to discuss how the access came together.

"Walk us through this," the anchor said. "Getting any time with the First Family is difficult enough, but this feels like a particularly intimate look. How did Essence make this happen?"

The editor-in-chief leaned forward, measured but clearly proud. "It came down to relationships and trust, honestly. We've spent years building a rapport with the administration, and more importantly, demonstrating that Essence understands how to tell this story with the dignity and depth it deserves. This wasn't just about getting a photo—it was about capturing something real."

"And how did the family respond to the idea?" the anchor pressed. "Was there hesitation, given how scrutinized their lives already are?"

"There's always some hesitation—that's natural," the editor-in-chief replied. "But I think they recognized that Essence has always been a platform of authenticity for Black families, Black culture, Black joy. This wasn't about a sensational angle. We wanted people to see the family as they are—warm, connected, human. I believe that resonated with them."

The anchor nodded. "There's clearly a symbolic weight to this. What does it mean for Essence to be the outlet trusted with these images?"

"It means everything," the editor-in-chief said. "For decades, Essence has told stories that mainstream media often overlooked or got wrong. To have this family—who represents so much hope and possibility for our community—trust us with this moment is deeply meaningful. It's a full-circle moment for our readers, who have followed this journey from the very beginning."

**Cultural Significance**

Media analysts noted that the exclusive underscored Essence's enduring role as a trusted voice within Black media, even as the broader media landscape has become increasingly fragmented and competitive. The photographs, once published, were shared widely across social media platforms, with many praising the warmth and intimacy captured in the images.

For longtime readers, the moment reaffirmed something the magazine has represented for generations: a space where Black stories—especially those of historic significance—are told with nuance, respect, and cultural fluency that larger, more mainstream outlets often struggle to achieve.

As the editor-in-chief noted before wrapping up the interview, "This is what Essence has always done. We tell our own stories, in our own way. And this was one we were honored to tell."
